text: So for those who don't know, Conductor is a desktop app for managing a team of coding agents all at the same time.

text: So instead of having a bunch of terminal windows for your cloud codes or your codexes or your whatever coding agent, you have one interface to manage them all.

speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so I thought I would compile a bunch of the principles that I've seen the best engineers use and give them to you all.

speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And here are my principles for being the fastest builder in your organization.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So, let's start with number one, stay near the frontier.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Staying near the frontier means you are always trying the latest things, basically the day they come out.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It means that when UltraCode comes out, you're trying it.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It means that when SlashGoal comes out, you're giving it a go.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It's really important to stay near the frontier for a few reasons.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: If you are doing your own startup, then staying near the frontier means that you will come up with lots of new ideas for what you should actually be building.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And this literally happened to us.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We were building a totally different app called Chorus.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: But we started using, we were such power users of Claude Code back in February of last year that we started building our whole workflow around Claude Code and we started cloning our repo five times and then we discovered work trees and then bit by bit we had built Conductor as an internal tool and we couldn't have figured that out if we weren't staying near the frontier.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And if you're not doing a startup, you should be the person at your company who always knows what the latest workflows are.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It used to be that you could just kind of use your social graph and the information that was important about the best workflows to use would trickle down to you, but things just move way too fast now.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You're always going to be three to six months behind if you do that.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So it's very important to stay near the frontier.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And there's an important word here, near.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: There is a danger if you are at the frontier.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You can do what I call midwit memeing, where you're spending all of your time working on your workflow and not doing actual work.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so internally we've come up with a heuristic for this.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We call it don't beat the market.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Don't try and beat the market.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The concept here, the heuristic you should use when you're trying to decide if you're near the frontier or at the frontier and too deep into the latest trends is you should ask yourself,
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Why isn't this workflow the default?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So, for example, when RALF loops were becoming a big thing, you should ask yourself, like, should I spend a ton of time optimizing my workflow to work with RALF loops?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Because
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: If route loops work for everyone, like if they are the default, then you probably should just wait for Anthropic or OpenAI or whatever to build the workflow into the default harness.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You can think of this as sort of like an efficient market hypothesis where unless you have like real alpha,
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You shouldn't be optimizing your workflow too much.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And what I mean by real alpha is some kind of information about either your users or your code base that the models might not know about.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So, an example for us is we're a chat app.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We have to render really long chats really quickly, and performance is important to us.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so, we need to spend a lot of time optimizing our React queries to render the chats quickly.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And we're willing to make sacrifices
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: and other parts of our code base to make that happen.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So, if you have some kind of alpha, it's like some kind of information about the app you're building that the models might not know about, then you should put time into the workflow.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Otherwise, don't midwet meme, don't be the person who has an amazing Emacs setup but doesn't actually get stuff done.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Okay, three.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Create slot-free zones.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So, at Conductor, we have this term we call a slot-free zone.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And a slot-free zone is a part of the code base or a part of the app that requires really strict human review.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And we're actually, I think, a little bit unusual in this way.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: I think a lot of people assume that we are
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Pure token maxers, and we are ripping through 30,000 line PRs, but we're actually not.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We're actually quite careful with certain parts of our codebase, and then very loose with other parts of our codebase.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The reason this is important is because if you are not careful about your slot-free zones, your codebase can get in a really...
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Tricky spot.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And this actually happened to us.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We've had to rewrite our whole app a couple of times because we weren't careful about slot-free zones.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Specifically, we have a migrations file.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And in our CI,
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Any change to the migrations file requires a human to review it.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We also assume that anything written in Slack is slop-free.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It's not written by the AI.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It's written by a human.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: All of our docs, our Claude MDs, all our skills, we put a ton of time into making them good.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And this is also something I've seen with all the best builders up close.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: They put an unusual amount of time into the Claude MD or their skill files.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And I think another way that I've thought about this is if you had a new intern that was joining your company,
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And you had the opportunity to like whisper something in their ear every time they started working.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Like every day, any time they sat down, you could like whisper something in their ear.

speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It's like information that gets loaded into the agent's context every time they start working.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so you probably want to put a lot of thought into those.

text: Okay, four.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Feed the beast.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: At Conductor we have an internal tool we call the Conductor Internal Agent.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And it is also known as the CIA.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And the CIA is basically the centralized database of everything that's happening in the organization.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So anytime a new Slack message gets sent,
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The CIA picks it up.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The CIA agent will see that a new message is sent in Slack.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It will pick it up and it will save it to a Postgres table.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Any time a user has a bug request in Discord, the same thing happens.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Any time we have a meeting, we are recording it and it goes into the CIA.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We call this Feed the Beast because you want to
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: For your agents to be effective in your company, you want them to have as much information and as much context as they can have about the way you guys specifically work.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And the best way to do that is by having a centralized place for all the information to go.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: I think this tweet sums it up pretty well.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It's really effective to just put everything in a database and then give your agent a SQL tool and let it handle the rest.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Okay, next is Free Range Agents.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Give your agents a lot of space to play.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Give them a sandbox that won't get killed, where they can explore your code base, where they can work on really hard tasks, where they know that they're not going to get shut down when you close your laptop lid.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Give them opportunities to create more of themselves.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Give them ways to collaborate with other agents and other humans.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: I think what's really interesting about free range agents and this concept and why this is important is the models are getting better and they are able to run for much longer and there are going to be many more of them.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so, if they are confined to your laptop, then they're not going to be nearly as effective as if they are free roaming.

text: The final principle that I want to talk about today, and the title of this talk is Orchestras, Not Factories.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The whole talk track today is about software factories, and I honestly kind of hate the term.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: I think it's the wrong way of thinking about these new tools that are emerging.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: When I think of a factory, I think of automation, and I think of, there's a lot of amazing things about automation, and it makes our lives more efficient, and we can create more of everything.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: I don't want the future to be built around factories.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: I want the future to, I want to feel like a human.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: I want to be in the flow.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: I want to be in front of an orchestra, waving my baton, and I wave it this way, and this team of agents starts working, and then this intermingling of humans and agents starts working as I go here.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And when I want to, I can zoom in on the details, but most of the time I can zoom out.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And I don't think the future should be we are like managing swarms of agents and we are like factory line managers like pushing buttons, getting the agents to like pump out the next feature.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

speaker: SPEAKER_00
